Outside of large firms where the particle accelerator market is a secondary focus, most suppliers are highly reliant on a smaller number of consistent, high-value contracts. New facilities outside of the national lab space are also subject to high levels of regulatory oversight, withnewisotopemanufacturingandenergyresearchfacilitiesoftennavigatingacomplexandconflictingset of regulatory agencies and safety requirements. Lack of expertise of some regulatory authorities in working with accelerator facilities can also be problematic. Much of the ML research in the accelerator space is still being performed within the national lab in- frastructure, centered at a couple facilities in particular, with strong leadership being provided by a small number of individuals. Industry involvement is minimal, with no official industry organization existing for equipment and services suppliers, and only a few boutique firms specializing in ML usage in the accelerator space. LargerML-specificfirmsarebeginningtoexpressinterestinincreasedparticipation,butlongfunding lead times and policy requirements, with minimal incentives from accelerator facilities and operators, make this challenging. There is an inherent conflict between the goals of the funding agencies and the goals of the organizations performing the work. Policy-level organizations have broad scientific and/or security goals. These goals do not mesh well with the needs of long-term operations at a multi-disciplinary facility that sometimes operates across multiple funding agencies. AI/ML research for operations falls squarely into this priorities gap, despite its increasing importance for maximizing accelerator uptime and usage. AI/ML research in process engineering can be seen in other market sectors, such as large-scale energy systems. Recent changes in policy may help re-prioritize the use of overhead and line item budgets for the devel- opment of collaborative software tools across facilities and industry, but the future is uncertain. Without a re-prioritization to focus on AI/ML in operations across all interested parties, it is likely that trained personnel will not be available in the workforce outside of AI and ML subject-matter experts in specialized firms. Privacy and security concerns for data sharing also need to be addressed if a collaboration is to be successful between disparate entities, both national and international. One long-term decision made on some AI/ML projects in the accelerator community will help buffer projects from drastic policy swings – third-party software repository ownership to avoid possible loss of code availability. 2.7 Introduction to AI/ML usage In machine learning, having an agreement for how data is stored and handled is critical. In the larger world ofmachinelearning,severalstandardsalreadyexist,usuallydrivenbywhatproprietarytoolsarebeingused by the industrial partners involved. For example, Google developed Tensorflow, Meta developed pytorch, and Microsoft and Apache both have different model storage standards, ONNX and TVM, respectively. Higher level frameworks include Keras, initially developed by a Google engineer, and the OpenAI/Farama Foundation Gym and Gymnasium, respectively. Each of these have developed with different licensing and development structures, leaving no ‘optimal’ choice for any particular use case.
